items.classSummary: Session 1: Why corporates and startups need each other. Corporates have money, distribution, brand, data and regulatory know-how but move slowly and struggle to innovate outside their core. Startups have speed, focus and new technology but lack customers, capital and credibility. Collaboration tries to combine the two. We discussed the 'dinosaur and the mouse' asymmetry and why most collaborations fail on mismatched expectations rather than technology.
items.unclearQuestion: If a large corporation already has substantial capital and engineering capacity, what prevents it from simply replicating a startup's idea rather than partnering with it? Is that legally permissible, and how should a startup decide how much to disclose?
keyPoints: Corporates bring capital, distribution, brand, data and regulatory know-how but innovate slowly outside their core
Startups bring speed, focus and new technology but lack customers, capital and credibility
Collaboration aims to combine these complementary strengths
Most collaborations fail on mismatched expectations rather than on the technology
items.tutorReply: That is a central question for any founder. Legally, a corporation can develop a similar product unless the startup's work is protected by patents, trade secrets or a signed NDA. In practice, replication is harder than it appears: the startup's real advantage is often speed, a team that has worked on the problem for years, and many small learnings that are not visible in a demo. Large firms also face internal hurdles such as budgets, competing priorities and risk committees, so building in-house can take two to three years while partnering can take months. That is why many corporates prefer to pilot, invest or acquire. Startups protect themselves by sharing what they do before how they do it, using NDAs, and choosing partners with a record of fair dealing.
followUps: What information should a startup withhold in an initial meeting with a corporate?
Are there documented cases of corporates replicating a startup's product after a pilot?
If replication is difficult, why do corporates continue to invest heavily in internal R&D?

thread.question: What information should a startup withhold in an initial meeting with a corporate? Specifically, should it share source code, its customer list or its pricing?
thread.tutorReply: It is sensible to settle this before the meeting. In a first meeting, share the problem you solve, the outcomes you have achieved (for example, reducing onboarding time by 40 percent for a bank) and a demonstration of the product's behaviour. Hold back source code, model weights and architecture details, your full customer list and contract terms, and anything that reveals how you achieve the result. Pricing can be shared as a range. A simple rule is to show what the corporate needs in order to decide whether to continue the conversation, and nothing more. Deeper technical disclosure should wait for a mutual NDA and a defined use case, which is a major theme of Session 9.
followUps: Is a mutual NDA realistically enforceable against a large corporation?
How can a startup demonstrate an AI product without revealing how it works?

thread.question: Is a mutual NDA realistically enforceable against a large corporation, given the difference in legal resources?
thread.tutorReply: It is enforceable in principle, but enforcement is costly and slow, so its main value lies in deterrence and clarity. A well-drafted NDA defines precisely what is confidential, how long the obligation lasts and what the receiving party may use the information for. Large corporations generally take NDAs seriously because a public breach would damage their reputation with the startup ecosystem they rely on for deal flow. The practical lesson is that an NDA reduces risk but does not remove it, so startups should still disclose progressively and keep records of what was shared and when.
followUps: How long should confidentiality obligations in an NDA typically last?
What records should a startup keep of what it has disclosed?

items.text: Question for the next session: in practice, which party usually initiates a corporate-startup relationship? Do startups typically approach corporates directly, or do corporates run dedicated scouting teams?

items.classSummary: Session 2: Open innovation. Henry Chesbrough's idea that firms should use external as well as internal ideas and paths to market. Outside-in: bringing external knowledge in (licensing, partnerships, crowdsourcing). Inside-out: letting unused internal ideas go out (spin-offs, out-licensing). Coupled: co-creation with partners. Examples included P&G's Connect + Develop and corporates licensing idle patents.
items.unclearQuestion: If open innovation involves sharing ideas with external parties, how does a firm protect its competitive advantage? How does 'open' differ from simply giving knowledge away, and is open innovation the same as open source?
keyPoints: Open innovation means using external as well as internal ideas and paths to market
Outside-in brings external knowledge in through licensing, partnerships and crowdsourcing
Inside-out lets unused internal ideas out through spin-offs and out-licensing
Coupled innovation is co-creation with partners, e.g. P&G's Connect + Develop
items.tutorReply: You have identified the central tension in the concept. Open does not mean free; it means the company stops assuming that every good idea must be invented and commercialised inside its own walls. Ideas flow in both directions, but usually through contracts such as licences, revenue shares or equity in spin-offs. Procter and Gamble did not give its secrets away with Connect + Develop; it published problems it wanted solved and paid the outsiders who solved them. Inside-out innovation is often about earning revenue from patents that would otherwise sit unused. Open innovation is also distinct from open source: open source is a licensing model in which code is publicly available, whereas open innovation is a broader strategy that can remain entirely proprietary.
followUps: How does a firm decide which capabilities are core and must remain closed?
Can a startup originate as an inside-out spin-off from a corporate?
What are the risks of publishing a problem on a crowdsourcing platform?

thread.question: How does a firm decide which capabilities are core and must remain closed, and which can be shared?
thread.tutorReply: Firms usually begin from their source of competitive advantage. Capabilities that customers pay a premium for, that are hard to imitate and that underpin future products tend to stay closed. Capabilities that are necessary but not differentiating, such as many testing, data-processing or manufacturing steps, are good candidates for partnering or licensing. A useful test from the session is to ask whether the firm would lose its position if a competitor had the same capability tomorrow; if so, it is core. The decision is not permanent, because as markets mature a once-core capability can become a commodity worth licensing out.
followUps: How do firms value an unused patent before licensing it?
Can opening up a capability ever create a new competitive advantage?

thread.question: Can a startup originate as an inside-out spin-off from a corporate, and how is ownership usually arranged in that case?
thread.tutorReply: Yes, and it is one of the clearest examples of inside-out open innovation. When a corporation holds a technology that does not fit its core business, it can license it to a new company formed by former employees or external founders. Ownership arrangements vary: the parent often keeps a minority equity stake, receives royalties, or both, while the founders and outside investors hold the majority so that the venture can raise capital and move quickly. The key points to negotiate are the scope of the licence, whether the parent has a right to buy the company back later, and how far the spin-off may rely on the parent's brand and customers.
followUps: Why would a parent company prefer a minority stake over full ownership of a spin-off?
What happens to a spin-off's licence if the parent company is acquired?

items.classSummary: Session 3: The engagement spectrum. Corporates can engage startups in many ways, from light-touch to deep commitment: events and hackathons, innovation challenges, pilots and proofs of concept, venture clienting (buying the startup's product), accelerator programmes, corporate venture capital investment, and finally M&A. Each mode differs in cost, control, speed and risk. Companies often use several at once.
items.unclearQuestion: What strategic value do corporates obtain from hackathons, beyond publicity? And how do they decide between buying a startup's product, investing in the startup, or acquiring it outright?
keyPoints: Corporates engage startups across a spectrum from light-touch to deep commitment
Modes include events and hackathons, challenges, pilots, venture clienting, accelerators, CVC and M&A
Each mode differs in cost, control, speed and risk
Companies often run several engagement modes at the same time
items.tutorReply: Publicity is part of it, but well-run hackathons serve real purposes: they scout talent and startups at low cost, test whether internal data or APIs are usable by outsiders, and signal to the ecosystem that the company is open to partners. There is no single official decision tree, but a useful rule of thumb is this. If the corporate mainly needs the solution, it buys it through venture clienting or a pilot. If it wants a window on a market and the option to go deeper later, it takes a minority stake through its CVC. If the capability is strategic and control matters, it acquires. Cost and commitment rise along that spectrum, so firms usually start light and move deeper only when the evidence justifies it.
followUps: Has a hackathon ever led directly to an acquisition?
What are the risks of moving straight to an acquisition?
Can a startup decline investment but still become a supplier?

thread.question: Can a startup decline a corporate's investment offer but still become its supplier, without damaging the relationship?
thread.tutorReply: Yes, and many founders choose this deliberately. Taking a corporate's money can create signalling problems: competitors of that corporate may refuse to buy from the startup, and later investors may worry that the corporate holds special rights. Being a supplier keeps the startup neutral. Professional corporate venture teams understand this, and a partner that reacts badly is revealing something about how the partnership would be run. A constructive approach is to propose earning the corporate's business as a customer first and revisiting investment once value has been proven together. That keeps the door open without locking the startup in.
followUps: What special rights do corporate investors typically request?
Do startups ever regret declining corporate investment?

thread.question: What are the risks for a corporate of moving directly to an acquisition without a pilot or minority investment first?
thread.tutorReply: The main risk is paying for an assumption that has not been tested. Without a pilot, the acquirer does not know whether the technology works inside its own systems, whether its business units will actually adopt it, or whether the startup's team will stay. Integration is the second risk: many acquired startups lose their speed once absorbed into corporate processes, and key founders leave when their earn-outs end. This is why the session described the engagement spectrum as a ladder. Each earlier step, from pilot to minority stake, reduces uncertainty before the largest and least reversible commitment.
followUps: What is an earn-out and why is it used in startup acquisitions?
How do acquirers retain startup founders after a deal?

items.classSummary: Session 4: Corporate accelerators and incubators. Corporates run time-bound programmes (usually 3–6 months) that give cohorts of startups mentoring, access to business units, data and sometimes funding, often in exchange for equity or first rights to partner. Incubators work with earlier-stage ideas over longer periods. We compared equity-based and equity-free models and discussed why many corporate accelerators shut down within a few years.
items.unclearQuestion: Why would a startup give up equity in exchange for mentoring, when general business advice is widely available for free? Given how many corporate accelerators close within a few years, is joining one a risk in itself?
keyPoints: Corporate accelerators are time-bound programmes of roughly 3–6 months for startup cohorts
They offer mentoring, access to business units and data, and sometimes funding
Startups often give equity or first partnership rights in return
Incubators work with earlier-stage ideas over longer periods
Equity-based and equity-free models differ, and many corporate accelerators close within a few years
items.tutorReply: Generic mentoring is indeed easy to find. What startups actually pay for in a good corporate accelerator is access: a named business-unit sponsor, real data to test on, faster procurement and a credible reference for the next sales conversation. If a programme cannot demonstrate that access, giving up equity is a poor exchange, which is why equity-free models have grown. Closures are not automatically a warning sign, but three checks are worthwhile before joining: whether there is a business-unit sponsor with budget, how many past cohort companies obtained paid contracts, and whether the programme reports to someone senior. Programmes that exist mainly for publicity are the ones most likely to disappear.
followUps: What does innovation theatre look like in practice?
What equity stake is typical for a corporate accelerator?
Can a startup join accelerators run by competing corporates?

thread.question: What does 'innovation theatre' look like in practice, and how can a startup recognise it early?
thread.tutorReply: Innovation theatre is activity that resembles innovation but is not connected to any business decision. Typical signs are demo days attended by senior executives but no budget holders, pilots without success criteria, and programmes measured by the number of startups admitted rather than the number of contracts signed. A startup can test for it early with three questions: which business unit will own the outcome, what budget is reserved for a rollout, and how many previous cohort companies became paying suppliers. Vague answers to all three are a strong warning sign.
followUps: Why do corporates run innovation theatre if it produces few results?
How should the success of an accelerator be measured?

thread.question: What equity stake is typical for a corporate accelerator, and is it negotiable?
thread.tutorReply: Equity-based corporate accelerators commonly ask for a small stake, often in the low single digits of percent, sometimes alongside a modest cash investment. Many corporate programmes are now equity-free and seek first access to partnerships or a right of first negotiation instead. Terms are usually standardised across a cohort, so the percentage itself is rarely negotiable, but the associated rights often are: exclusivity, information rights and rights of first refusal deserve close reading. A startup should weigh the stake against concrete benefits, such as a guaranteed paid pilot or access to data, rather than against the programme's reputation.
followUps: Why are rights of first refusal a concern for future acquirers?
How do equity-free accelerators justify their cost to the corporate?

items.text: Point to raise in the CVC session: if equity-free accelerators exist, what is the corporate's return on them? My working assumption is early access to partnerships and reputational benefit, but I would like to confirm this.

items.classSummary: Session 5: Corporate venture capital. CVC units invest corporate money in external startups, usually minority stakes. Objectives can be strategic (window on technology, new markets, complementary products) or financial (returns), and most CVCs try to balance both. We looked at how strategic CVCs judge success differently from independent VCs and at examples like Intel Capital and Google Ventures.
items.unclearQuestion: If a CVC invests the company's own money, why are financial returns important? Is the strategic objective not the main purpose, and who determines whether a CVC has been successful?
keyPoints: CVC units invest corporate money in external startups, usually as minority stakes
Objectives can be strategic (technology window, new markets, complementary products) or financial
Most CVCs try to balance strategic and financial goals
Strategic CVCs judge success differently from independent VCs, e.g. Intel Capital and Google Ventures
items.tutorReply: This is an important distinction. Financial returns matter for two reasons. The first is credibility: a CVC that loses money is easy for the CFO to close in a difficult year, so returns protect the strategic mission. The second is discipline: pursuing strategic value without return expectations can lead to overpaying for fashionable startups. Success is usually judged by a combination of the CVC's investment committee, the business units it is meant to serve and the CFO. Well-run CVCs agree in advance on strategic measures, such as the number of portfolio companies that become suppliers or partners, alongside financial measures such as internal rate of return, so that success is not assessed loosely after the fact.
followUps: What happens to portfolio companies when a corporate closes its CVC?
Why might a startup prefer a CVC over an independent VC?
How is a CVC partner compensated compared with an independent VC partner?

thread.question: What happens to portfolio startups when a corporate closes its CVC unit? Are they expected to return the investment?
thread.tutorReply: No, the investment does not have to be returned. It is equity, so the startup keeps the cash and the corporate keeps its shares. What usually happens is less dramatic but still significant: the corporate stops making follow-on investments, its board seat may become inactive, and the internal champions who connected the startup to business units move on. Sometimes the corporate sells the whole portfolio to a secondary buyer. This is why founders ask how long a CVC has existed, whether it has its own committed fund and whether it has survived a downturn, topics that Session 6 covers in more detail.
followUps: What is a secondary buyer for a venture portfolio?
Does a dedicated fund protect startups better than balance-sheet investing?

thread.question: Why might a startup prefer a CVC over an independent VC, given the potential conflicts of interest?
thread.tutorReply: The main attraction is access that an independent VC cannot offer: a potential first customer, distribution channels, technical expertise and credibility with other large buyers. A CVC may also be more patient, because its parent values strategic learning as well as financial return. The trade-offs are the conflicts you mention. Competitors of the parent may hesitate to buy from the startup, and the CVC's interests may diverge from other investors' interests in an acquisition. Founders often manage this by taking CVC money alongside independent VCs, limiting the CVC's special rights and ensuring that the corporate does not control the board.
followUps: Which special rights should founders resist when a CVC invests?
Can one startup take investment from two competing corporates?

items.classSummary: Session 6: CVC structures and governance. CVCs can invest directly from the balance sheet, through a dedicated fund with committed capital, or as a limited partner in an external VC fund. We discussed investment committees, how independent the CVC team should be from business units, compensation (carry vs salary/bonus), and how structure affects speed of decision-making and longevity.
items.unclearQuestion: Why would a corporate invest through an external VC fund as a limited partner rather than investing directly? Could you also clarify what 'carried interest' means?
keyPoints: CVCs can invest from the balance sheet, through a dedicated fund, or as an LP in an external VC fund
Investment committees and the CVC team's independence from business units shape governance
Compensation can be carry-based or salary-and-bonus
Structure affects decision speed and how long the CVC survives
items.tutorReply: It can be a sensible first step. Investing as a limited partner in an external fund lets a corporate learn the market, see a wide range of deals and build relationships without hiring a full investment team, and it often precedes setting up its own CVC. Carried interest is the share of investment profits, typically around 20 percent, paid to the people managing the fund once investors have received their capital back. Many CVCs do not offer carried interest and pay salary and bonus instead, which makes it harder to retain experienced investors. That is one reason dedicated, more independent fund structures tend to attract stronger teams and last longer.
followUps: Why do few corporates offer carried interest to their CVC teams?
How quickly can a balance-sheet CVC approve an investment?
Who typically sits on a CVC investment committee?

thread.question: Why do relatively few corporates offer carried interest to their CVC teams?
thread.tutorReply: There are several reasons. Carried interest can produce payouts larger than senior executives' salaries, which raises internal fairness and governance concerns. It also sits awkwardly with balance-sheet investing, where there is no separate fund with a defined profit pool. Finally, many corporates want the CVC team to prioritise strategic value, whereas carried interest rewards financial returns. The consequence, discussed in class, is that corporates without it struggle to hire and keep experienced investors, so some have moved to dedicated funds with partial carry or long-term bonuses linked to fund performance.
followUps: How do dedicated CVC funds differ from balance-sheet investing?
Does paying carried interest make a CVC behave more like an independent VC?

thread.question: Who typically sits on a CVC investment committee, and how does its composition affect the speed of decisions?
thread.tutorReply: A typical committee includes the head of the CVC, a finance representative such as the CFO or a delegate, the head of corporate strategy and senior leaders from the relevant business units. Some committees add an external venture investor for an independent view. A larger committee with many business-unit voices gives stronger strategic alignment but tends to slow decisions, because each member may need internal sign-off. Startups notice this directly: a CVC that takes three months to approve a seed investment can lose deals to independent VCs. Many CVCs therefore delegate smaller investments to a narrower group within agreed limits.
followUps: How long does a CVC typically take to approve an investment compared with an independent VC?
How can a CVC keep business units involved without slowing decisions?

items.classSummary: Session 7: Venture clienting, pilots and proofs of concept. Venture clienting means the corporate becomes a paying customer of the startup instead of an investor. Pilots and POCs test a solution on a small scale. Many collaborations get stuck in 'pilot purgatory' — endless unpaid or small pilots that never scale. We covered success criteria, paid pilots, business-unit ownership and a defined path to a full contract.
items.unclearQuestion: Why would a startup accept an unpaid pilot, which appears to amount to free consulting for a large company? At what point should a startup stop running pilots and decline further work?
keyPoints: Venture clienting means the corporate becomes a paying customer rather than an investor
Pilots and proofs of concept test a solution at small scale
Many collaborations get stuck in 'pilot purgatory' and never scale
Clear success criteria, paid pilots, business-unit ownership and a path to contract help avoid it
items.tutorReply: The concern is well founded. Early-stage startups accept unpaid pilots because the reference customer, the case study and the real-world data can be valuable, but only if there is a clear path to a contract. The warning signs of pilot purgatory are the absence of a named business-unit owner with budget, the absence of written success criteria, and a request to extend a pilot that has already succeeded. A sound rule is to agree in writing, before starting, which result triggers a paid rollout. As for how many pilots are too many: if a second pilot with the same corporate is proposed without new learning goals, or a pilot runs beyond roughly three to six months without a purchasing decision, the startup should press for a contract or withdraw.
followUps: How should a startup price a paid pilot?
What should written success criteria for a pilot contain?
Can a startup charge for a pilot after an earlier unpaid one?

thread.question: What should written success criteria for a pilot contain, in concrete terms?
thread.tutorReply: A one-page pilot charter usually contains six elements: the business problem in the corporate's own words; two or three measurable targets, for example reducing invoice-processing time from five days to two across 500 invoices; the baseline and how it will be measured, and by whom; the duration and the data or systems access the startup will receive; named owners on both sides; and the decision trigger, stating that if the targets are met the business unit will begin procurement for a rollout within 30 days. Both sides sign it. The final element is what prevents pilot purgatory, because it turns an experiment into a commitment.
followUps: Who on the corporate side should sign the pilot charter?
What should happen if the corporate changes the targets during the pilot?

thread.question: Who on the corporate side should sign the pilot charter for it to carry real weight?
thread.tutorReply: Ideally two people sign. The first is the business-unit owner who holds the budget for a rollout, because that signature connects the pilot to a purchasing decision. The second is the operational lead who will run the pilot day to day and control access to data and systems. Where the pilot involves regulated data, someone from IT security or compliance should approve the scope at the start rather than raising objections at the end. A signature from the innovation team alone is a weak signal, since innovation teams rarely hold rollout budgets.
followUps: How can a startup identify the real budget holder early?
What happens if the business-unit owner changes during the pilot?

items.text: Discussion point from our group: is pilot purgatory mainly the corporate's responsibility or the startup's? Harry argued the corporate's, and Naman the startup's for not insisting on a contract. I think both share responsibility; I will raise this in Session 8.

items.classSummary: Session 8: Global Capability Centres (GCCs) in India. Multinationals run GCCs in cities like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Gurugram, which have evolved from back-office cost centres into hubs for engineering, R&D and product innovation. Many GCCs now run startup engagement programmes, partner with local startups and act as a bridge between Indian startups and global headquarters.
items.unclearQuestion: Is a Global Capability Centre essentially an outsourcing office under a different name? If a startup partners with a GCC in Bengaluru, does that partnership typically reach global headquarters?
keyPoints: Multinationals run GCCs in Indian cities such as Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Gurugram
GCCs have evolved from back-office cost centres into hubs for engineering, R&D and product innovation
Many GCCs now run startup engagement programmes and partner with local startups
GCCs can act as a bridge between Indian startups and global headquarters
items.tutorReply: That was a fair description fifteen to twenty years ago. The difference from outsourcing is that a GCC is owned by the multinational itself, so its staff are employees working on the company's own products rather than a vendor's staff. Many GCCs now own global products or platforms end to end. Whether a startup partnership reaches headquarters depends on the GCC's mandate. Useful questions are whether the GCC owns a global product line or budget, whether there is a named global sponsor, and whether a previous startup partner has been rolled out in other countries. Where the answers are positive, the GCC is an accessible entry point with local leadership and faster meetings; where they are not, the partnership risks remaining a local showcase.
followUps: How can a startup identify which GCC teams hold global budgets?
Do GCCs usually contract with startups in rupees or in dollars?
How do GCC startup programmes differ from corporate accelerators?

thread.question: How can a startup identify which GCC teams hold global budgets or product ownership?
thread.tutorReply: Start with public signals: job postings that mention global product ownership, leadership titles such as global head based in India, and announcements of products launched from the centre. In conversations, ask directly who approves spending on a rollout beyond India and whether the team has previously taken an external solution into other regions. GCC startup programmes often publish their sponsoring business units, which also helps. Alumni of the programme are another good source, since they can say whether their pilots stayed local or scaled globally.
followUps: What questions should a startup ask in a first meeting with a GCC?
How long does a GCC pilot usually take to scale globally?

thread.question: How do GCC startup programmes differ from corporate accelerators run at headquarters?
thread.tutorReply: GCC programmes are usually more operational and closer to delivery. They tend to focus on solving specific problems for the centre's engineering or product teams, often through paid pilots, rather than offering broad mentoring or equity investment. They also have practical advantages for Indian startups: the same time zone, local contracting entities and easier in-person meetings. The limitation is mandate. Headquarters accelerators may have closer links to group strategy and CVC funds, while the reach of a GCC programme depends on how much global ownership the centre holds.
followUps: Do GCC programmes ever lead to CVC investment?
How does a GCC's mandate typically evolve over time?

items.classSummary: Session 9: Legal foundations. We went through the main documents in corporate-startup deals: NDAs (mutual vs one-way), term sheets for investments, master services agreements (MSAs) and statements of work for supplier relationships, plus clauses on exclusivity, rights of first refusal, liability and termination. Startups often lack legal resources and sign standard corporate templates without negotiating.
items.unclearQuestion: If the corporate's lawyers draft the contract, is the agreement inevitably weighted against the startup? Can a small startup negotiate effectively, and which clause deserves the closest scrutiny?
keyPoints: Core documents include NDAs, investment term sheets, MSAs and statements of work
NDAs can be mutual or one-way
Key clauses cover exclusivity, rights of first refusal, liability and termination
Startups often sign standard corporate templates without negotiating
items.tutorReply: It is a question worth settling early. Corporate templates are written to protect the corporate, but they are usually a starting point rather than a final offer. Small startups negotiate successfully by being specific: rather than calling a term unfair, they propose an alternative, such as capping liability at the contract value instead of leaving it unlimited. If one clause should never be signed without careful review, it is exclusivity, together with the related right of first refusal. Exclusivity can prevent a startup from selling to an entire industry, and a right of first refusal can deter future acquirers. Unlimited liability and broad IP assignment clauses follow closely, and Session 10 examines the latter in detail.
followUps: When does granting exclusivity make commercial sense?
What does a legal review of an MSA typically cost a startup?
How does a one-way NDA differ from a mutual NDA in practice?

thread.question: When, if ever, does granting exclusivity to a corporate make commercial sense?
thread.tutorReply: Exclusivity is a trade, so it should be priced like one. It can make sense when it is narrow, short and paid for: limited to one product category or region, lasting around twelve to eighteen months, and given in exchange for a guaranteed minimum purchase or meaningful revenue. A use-it-or-lose-it condition is also advisable, so that exclusivity ends automatically if the corporate does not reach agreed volumes. What a startup should avoid is broad, open-ended exclusivity given away simply to secure a well-known reference customer. A helpful test is whether the startup could survive with the clause in place if the partner became inactive for a year.
followUps: What is a minimum purchase commitment and how is it enforced?
Can exclusivity end early if the corporate breaches the agreement?

thread.question: How does a one-way NDA differ from a mutual NDA in practice, and which should a startup request?
thread.tutorReply: A one-way NDA protects only the disclosing party, whereas a mutual NDA protects information flowing in both directions. Corporates sometimes offer one-way NDAs that protect their own information but not the startup's, which is the wrong way round for a startup presenting its technology. In most collaborations both sides share something sensitive, so a mutual NDA is the reasonable default. The startup should also check the definition of confidential information, the duration, any residuals clause that allows the corporate to use what its staff remember, and whether the NDA restricts the startup from working with competitors.
followUps: What is a residuals clause and why is it risky?
Should an NDA ever restrict a startup from working with competitors?

items.classSummary: Session 10: IP risks. Background IP is what each party brings into the collaboration; foreground IP is what is created during it. Joint development raises questions about ownership, licensing rights, field-of-use restrictions and what happens when the partnership ends. We discussed cases where startups lost rights to their core technology through broad IP assignment clauses, and how licences can be used instead of assignment.
items.unclearQuestion: When a startup and a corporate jointly develop technology, who owns the result? If the corporate improves the startup's technology during the project, does it acquire rights over the original?
keyPoints: Background IP is what each party brings; foreground IP is created during the collaboration
Joint development raises questions about ownership, licensing, field-of-use and post-partnership rights
Broad IP assignment clauses have cost startups the rights to their core technology
Licences can be used instead of assignment to protect the startup
items.tutorReply: Ownership is not automatically shared equally; it depends entirely on the contract. Without careful drafting, joint ownership can be problematic, because in some jurisdictions each co-owner may exploit the result without the other's consent. A common startup-friendly structure is that each party keeps its background IP, the startup owns improvements to its own core technology, the corporate owns elements specific to its business such as integrations with internal systems, and the corporate receives a licence to use what it needs. If the corporate improves the startup's technology under a broad assignment clause, it could own those improvements, which is why the clause must be negotiated before any joint development begins.
followUps: What is a field-of-use restriction?
How can a startup evidence its background IP before a project starts?
Can a corporate patent jointly developed work without informing the startup?

thread.question: What is a field-of-use restriction, and how does it protect each party?
thread.tutorReply: A field-of-use restriction limits a licence to a defined application, market or industry. For example, a startup might license its image-recognition technology to a car manufacturer for use in vehicle safety systems only, while keeping the right to license the same technology to retailers or hospitals. The corporate obtains the rights it needs for its business, and the startup retains the freedom to grow in other markets. Precise drafting matters: a field described too broadly, such as transportation, can quietly cover markets the startup intended to pursue.
followUps: How should a startup define a field of use narrowly but workably?
Can a field-of-use restriction be renegotiated later?

thread.question: How can a startup evidence its background IP before a joint project begins?
thread.tutorReply: The standard approach is to list background IP in a schedule to the agreement, describing each technology, its version and any related patents or applications. The schedule should be supported by records such as dated source-code repositories, design documents, lab notebooks and filed patent applications. Some startups also deposit a snapshot of key code with a third party at the start of the project. The aim is to make it straightforward to prove, if a dispute arises, what existed before the collaboration and therefore what the corporate cannot claim as foreground IP.
followUps: Should a startup file patents before starting a joint project?
What is a code escrow arrangement?

items.text: Revision note for the group: background IP is what each party brings into a collaboration, and foreground IP is what is created during it. The agreement should list background IP in a schedule before any work begins.

items.classSummary: Session 11: Cultural gaps. Corporates and startups differ in speed, risk appetite, decision rights, planning horizons and attitude to failure. Corporate procurement, compliance and security reviews can take months, which can kill a startup's cash runway. We discussed boundary spanners, fast-track procurement and 'translators' who help both sides understand each other.
items.unclearQuestion: Why does a corporation take several months to approve a purchase order for a comparatively small pilot? Is this genuinely a matter of culture, or simply inefficiency? Also, what does a boundary spanner do in practice?
keyPoints: Corporates and startups differ in speed, risk appetite, decision rights, planning horizons and attitude to failure
Procurement, compliance and security reviews can take months and drain a startup's runway
Boundary spanners and 'translators' help each side understand the other
Fast-track procurement can reduce delays
items.tutorReply: The delay is real, but it is rarely simple inefficiency. Corporate processes are designed to manage risk at scale: a security review exists because one weak supplier can cause a breach affecting millions of customers, and procurement rules exist to prevent fraud and favouritism. The difficulty is that the same heavy process is applied to a five-lakh-rupee pilot and a five-hundred-crore contract. A boundary spanner is the person who works between the two worlds. They translate startup urgency into the corporate's language of risk, compliance and return, find the right approver, help the startup complete security questionnaires and push for fast-track procurement. An effective boundary spanner can save a startup several months.
followUps: How can a startup accelerate a security review from its own side?
Is a boundary spanner usually employed by the corporate or the startup?
What is fast-track procurement and who can approve it?

thread.question: How can a startup accelerate a security review from its own side?
thread.tutorReply: There is no shortcut, but preparation helps considerably. Prepare a security pack before anyone asks for it: a completed standard questionnaire, a data-flow diagram, where data is stored, encryption details, access controls and the incident-response process. Where affordable, certifications such as ISO 27001 or a SOC 2 report answer most questions at once. Offer an early call between the startup's technical lead and the corporate's security team, since many weeks are lost to email exchanges. Finally, scope the pilot to minimise risk, for example by using anonymised or synthetic data and avoiding production access, because a lower-risk pilot often qualifies for a lighter review.
followUps: How costly is ISO 27001 or SOC 2 certification for a startup?
What is the difference between anonymised and synthetic data?

thread.question: Is a boundary spanner usually employed by the corporate or by the startup?
thread.tutorReply: Most often the boundary spanner sits inside the corporate, typically in an innovation, venture or partnering team, because their value comes from knowing the internal decision-makers and processes. Startups benefit from having an equivalent on their own side, often a founder or an enterprise sales lead with corporate experience, who can translate the startup's needs into the corporate's language of risk and return. The most effective collaborations have one on each side working closely together. When the corporate boundary spanner is missing, the startup's lead has to carry the whole translation burden alone.
followUps: What skills make an effective boundary spanner?
How do corporates reward boundary spanners internally?

items.classSummary: Session 12: Partnership pitfalls. Common reasons collaborations fail: misaligned KPIs and incentives, the internal champion leaving or changing role, not-invented-here syndrome among corporate engineers, startups becoming dependent on one big customer, and unclear ownership after a pilot. We discussed warning signs and ways to de-risk each pitfall.
items.unclearQuestion: What happens to a partnership if the corporate champion who supported the startup leaves the company? This seems a fragile basis for a business relationship. Is 'not-invented-here' a genuine phenomenon or merely an excuse?
keyPoints: Misaligned KPIs and incentives commonly cause collaborations to fail
Losing the internal champion through a role change or exit can stall a partnership
Not-invented-here syndrome among corporate engineers creates resistance
Dependence on one big customer and unclear post-pilot ownership are major risks
items.tutorReply: The concern is justified: losing a champion is one of the most common reasons partnerships stall. The remedy is never to depend on a single champion. From the outset, build relationships at three levels: the day-to-day user, the business-unit budget owner and an executive sponsor. Record success in shared documents and dashboards so that the value survives a reorganisation, and when a champion leaves, ask them to introduce their successor before they go. Not-invented-here is a genuine phenomenon: engineers can see an external solution as a threat to their role or their professional pride. It is countered by involving internal teams early, giving them credit and positioning the startup as a tool that strengthens their work rather than replaces it.
followUps: How should a startup approach an executive sponsor without bypassing its champion?
What share of revenue from one customer is too concentrated?
Can not-invented-here ever benefit the corporate?

thread.question: How should a startup approach an executive sponsor without appearing to bypass its champion?
thread.tutorReply: Involve the champion in the process rather than going around them. Most champions also benefit from executive visibility, so the startup can propose a short results review with the sponsor that the champion presents, with the startup in support. Framing matters: the purpose is to secure the decision and budget the champion needs, not to escalate. If the champion is reluctant, that is useful information in itself, since it may indicate that they lack the authority to scale the partnership. Regular written updates addressed to both levels also keep the sponsor informed without any appearance of bypassing.
followUps: How often should a startup update an executive sponsor?
What should a results review with a sponsor contain?

thread.question: What share of revenue from a single customer should a startup consider too concentrated?
thread.tutorReply: There is no fixed rule, but many investors become concerned when a single customer accounts for more than about a third to a half of revenue. Above that level, losing the customer or a change in its priorities threatens the startup's survival, and the customer gains considerable pricing power. Early-stage startups often exceed this temporarily, which is acceptable if there is a credible plan to diversify. Contract terms also help: longer commitments, notice periods for termination and the freedom to sell to the customer's competitors all reduce the risk of concentration.
followUps: How do investors assess customer concentration during due diligence?
Should a startup ever deliberately accept a single anchor customer?

items.classSummary: Session 13: Designing and measuring partnerships, and course wrap-up. We pulled the course together: choose the engagement mode to fit the strategic goal, agree KPIs that matter to both sides (for example time-to-contract, adoption, revenue and learning), plan integration early, and define exit or scale-up paths in advance. We revisited open innovation, CVC, GCCs, legal and IP risks, cultural gaps and pitfalls as one connected framework.
items.unclearQuestion: Having completed the course, is corporate-startup collaboration generally worthwhile, or do most collaborations fail? If we were founders, would you recommend partnering with a large company?
keyPoints: Choose the engagement mode to fit the strategic goal
Agree KPIs that matter to both sides, such as time-to-contract, adoption, revenue and learning
Plan integration early and define exit or scale-up paths in advance
Open innovation, CVC, GCCs, legal and IP risks, cultural gaps and pitfalls form one connected framework
items.tutorReply: It is a fitting question to end the course with. Many individual collaborations do fail, but those that succeed can be transformational: a single corporate customer or partner can give a startup distribution that would take years to build alone. The central lesson of the course is that success is a matter of design rather than luck. As founders, it would be reasonable to pursue partnerships, provided you choose partners with a track record, begin with a paid and well-scoped pilot with written success criteria, protect your IP and avoid broad exclusivity, cultivate several champions, and ensure that no single corporate becomes too large a share of revenue. Doing so would already place you ahead of most founders entering these arrangements.
followUps: If you had to select one lesson from the course, which would it be?
What kinds of startups should be cautious about partnering with corporates?
How could we design our final project as a corporate-startup partnership?

thread.question: If you had to select one lesson from the thirteen sessions, which would it be?
thread.tutorReply: I would choose this: agree in writing what success looks like before the work begins. It addresses problems from almost every session. It prevents pilot purgatory (Session 7), keeps CVC objectives honest (Sessions 5 and 6), forces clarity on IP and exclusivity (Sessions 9 and 10), gives boundary spanners something concrete to move through procurement (Session 11) and helps a partnership survive the loss of a champion (Session 12). Most of the failed collaborations studied had good technology and good intentions; what they lacked was a shared, written definition of success.
followUps: Can you give an example of a success definition that was too vague?
Who should own the success definition, the startup or the corporate?

thread.question: What kinds of startups should be cautious about partnering with corporates?
thread.tutorReply: Caution is warranted for very early startups whose product is still changing rapidly, because a corporate partner's requirements can pull the roadmap towards one customer's needs. Startups whose main asset is easily copied know-how, rather than protected technology or data, face greater disclosure risk. Startups with a short cash runway should be wary of long sales cycles, since a slow procurement process can outlast their funding. Finally, startups whose ideal customers are competitors of the prospective partner should think carefully before accepting investment or exclusivity. None of these rule partnership out; they change how it should be structured.
followUps: How can an early-stage startup protect its roadmap in a corporate partnership?
How much runway should a startup have before entering a corporate sales cycle?

items.text: Closing reflection for our final project: the recurring theme across the course was that successful partnerships define success in writing before work begins. We should use this as the framing for our project proposal.
